309.title: The library that was lost
309.hook: the Sikh Reference Library, with old handwritten manuscripts, was lost in the operation's aftermath
309.howItsDone: Sikh institutions continue to ask for the return of manuscripts and documents from the Sikh Reference Library, and Sikhs remember its loss as part of the June remembrance each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghallughara: the army in the Harmandir complex on a holy day, the Akal Takht damaged, and your line, remember the pilgrims. Today, a quieter loss from the same days, one made of paper and ink. Day three hundred nine.

A letter from a great-grandparent. A wedding photograph gone brown at the edges. A recipe written in a hand nobody alive can match. If a fire took them, no shop could sell them back. Now widen that to a whole people: the handwriting of their history, some of it centuries old, kept in one building. That building stood inside the Harmandir complex until June 1984. Today: the library that was lost.
screen: `A LETTER, A PHOTOGRAPH, A RECIPE.` → `NO SHOP SELLS IT BACK.` → `A WHOLE BUILDING OF THEM.`

segments.voice: It was called the Sikh Reference Library, set up in the complex in the 1940s. What was in it? Handwritten copies of the Guru Granth Sahib, some very old, copied out by hand long before printing. Hukamnamas: letters of instruction to Sikh communities, some said to have been sent by the Gurus themselves. Rare books, old histories, documents of the Singh Sabha and the gurdwara reform movement. Scholars came from far away to read there. It was the memory of the community on shelves. In June 1984, the library burned. How it happened is disputed. The army's account says it caught fire during the fighting. Many Sikhs, and some witnesses, say the fighting had ended first, and that the building was burned afterward, and that boxes of material were carried away before the fire. Over the years, some items have been returned. Many have never been found. Sikh bodies still ask for the rest to be given back, and the question is still open. Why does a library matter so much, in a week when people died? Because the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru, and handwritten copies carried the Guru's word across generations. A hukamnama in a Guru's hand is a thread straight back to them. Losing them is like losing the family letters, except the family is a whole community. Memory, here, is not just knowledge. It is connection.
screen: `THE SIKH REFERENCE LIBRARY.` · `HANDWRITTEN GRANTHS AND HUKAMNAMAS.` · `IT BURNED; HOW IS DISPUTED.` · `THE GURU'S WORD, CARRIED BY HAND.` · then, large: `MEMORY IS PRECIOUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold something old. If you can, find an old book, a photograph, a letter, anything that carries someone's memory. Hold it in your hands. Look at it slowly: the paper, the handwriting, the wear at the corners. If there's nothing old nearby, picture one. Think of who made it, and who kept it safe so it could reach you. Let yourself be grateful to the keepers. Then rest with the breath, holding it gently. The bell holds the time.
Hukamnama. A letter of command from the Gurus — among the handwritten Granths and hukamnamas lost when the Sikh Reference Library burned after June 1984.
Your line: memory is precious. Today, save one family memory somewhere safe: scan a photo, write down a story, or ask someone older to tell it. Day three hundred nine.

310.title: November 1984
310.hook: after Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards, mobs killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi
310.howItsDone: Each November, Sikhs hold remembrance gatherings, Ardas and kirtan for those killed in 1984, and survivors and families read out names and tell their stories.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukamnama: handwritten Granths and the Gurus' letters, gone in a fire. Your line was memory is precious. Today we need that line, because today is about remembering people. Go gently. Day three hundred ten.

On the morning of the thirty-first of October, 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi walked through her garden in New Delhi toward an interview. Two of her own bodyguards, both Sikhs, shot her. She died that day. The news spread through the city in hours. By that evening, and over the next three days, something terrible happened, not to the two men, who were already in custody or dead, but to Sikh families who had nothing to do with it. Today: November 1984.

From the first of November, mobs moved through parts of Delhi and other cities, hunting Sikhs. They carried lists, or asked neighbors which houses were Sikh. Sikh men and boys were dragged out and killed, many of them burned. Homes, shops and gurdwaras were set on fire. Women were attacked. The worst was in poorer neighborhoods of east and west Delhi, where whole lanes lost their men. For days, the police largely failed to stop it, and in places stood by. Official figures later counted about twenty-seven hundred killed in Delhi alone, and more across India. Many Sikhs believe the true number was higher. Later inquiries and courts found that some local political leaders had led or encouraged the mobs. This was not a riot between two communities. It was violence against one community, for something two men had done. And here we hold our promise from the start of the week: no people as a whole are to blame. In those same lanes, there were Hindu families who hid Sikh neighbors in their homes, cut a boy's hair to save his life, or stood at the door and lied to the mob. Their courage is part of the story too. The line today is simple and heavy: they had names. The people killed were not a number. They were fathers and sons, a shopkeeper, a taxi driver, a teenager coming home. Survivors, many of them widows, have spent their lives making sure the names are said. Remembering someone by name is the smallest and most important thing we can do.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one minute of silence. Settle, and let your body be still. For one minute, say nothing and do nothing. Hold in mind the families of November 1984: the ones who died, and the ones who went on living without them. You don't need to picture anything terrible. Just keep them company in the quiet. When the minute is over, keep resting with the breath, and let the silence stay a little longer. The bell holds the time.
Yaad. Remembrance — after Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards, mobs killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi, in November 1984. They had names.
Your line: they had names. Today, when you hear a number of people harmed anywhere, pause and remember that each one was someone's person. Day three hundred ten.

311.title: The long wait
311.hook: survivors, many of them widows, waited decades for justice, while the years that followed brought violence to many Punjabi families of every background
311.howItsDone: Sikh organizations and families of 1984 survivors continue to press for justice through the courts, and each November gatherings remember the dead and the widows who waited.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yaad: thousands of Sikhs killed by mobs, and neighbors who hid neighbors. Your line was they had names. Today, the people who carried those names for decades after. Day three hundred eleven.

In west Delhi there's a neighborhood people have long called the Widow Colony. After November 1984, many women who had lost husbands, sons and brothers in a few days were moved there, into small flats, often with young children. They went to work. They raised their kids. And year after year, they went to hearings, stood in front of commissions, and told the same story again. Some of them grew old doing it. Some died before any court said a word. Today: the long wait.
screen: `THE WIDOW COLONY.` → `WORK, CHILDREN, HEARINGS.` → `YEAR AFTER YEAR.`

segments.voice: After November 1984, there were many inquiries. Commission after commission, committee after committee, around ten of them over twenty years. Reports were written. Few people were punished. In 2005, the Prime Minister, himself a Sikh, apologized in parliament. In 2018, more than thirty years later, a court sentenced a senior politician to life in prison for his part. For the widows, some of it came too late, and some has never come. And the long wait wasn't only in Delhi. In Punjab, the years after 1984 brought a decade of violence that reached families of every background. Armed militants killed many people: Hindus, Sikhs who opposed them, police, bus passengers. In 1985 a bomb on an Air India flight from Canada killed three hundred twenty-nine people; a Canadian inquiry blamed militants based in Canada, though only one man was ever convicted. And the state's response was harsh too: young Sikh men were detained, and many disappeared. A Sikh human rights worker named Jaswant Singh Khalra went through cremation records in Amritsar and found thousands of bodies burned as unidentified. In 1995 he was taken from outside his home and killed. Police officers were later convicted. So the wait belongs to many: widows in Delhi, mothers in Punjab still asking where a son went, families who lost someone to a militant's gun. Sikh teaching speaks of the Guru's justice, and of standing for the oppressed. And this is why the line matters: justice delayed still matters. A verdict after thirty years can't give anyone back. But it says out loud that a wrong was a wrong, and that the names count.
screen: `TEN INQUIRIES, FEW PUNISHED.` · `AN APOLOGY, A VERDICT, DECADES ON.` · `VIOLENCE FOR EVERY BACKGROUND.` · `KHALRA AND THE CREMATION RECORDS.` · then, large: `JUSTICE DELAYED STILL MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold those still waiting for justice. Settle, and breathe. Think of anyone, anywhere, who is still waiting: a family asking for answers, a person whose case is stuck, a community whose wrong was never named. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If you don't, simply keep them in mind, and wish them strength for the waiting. Notice if anger comes. Let it be there without feeding it. Then return to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Insaaf. Justice — the word on banners as survivors of 1984, many of them widows, waited decades for it, while violence reached Punjabi families of every background.
Your line: justice delayed still matters. Today, if someone tells you about a wrong done to them long ago, don't say move on. Say, that mattered. Day three hundred eleven.

312.title: How the panth remembers
312.hook: with ardas, kirtan and remembrance each June and November, and still chardi kala
312.howItsDone: Sikhs mark June and November 1984 with Ardas, kirtan and remembrance gatherings; like every Ardas, these end with the line asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, insaaf: widows in Delhi, families in Punjab, a verdict decades late. Your line was justice delayed still matters. Today, the last day of this heavy week: how the Sikh community carries all of it. Day three hundred twelve.

A gurdwara, on an evening in early June, or early November. The hall is full. The kirtan is slower than usual. Some people are crying quietly. A few older women sit near the front holding photographs. Then everyone stands, hands joined, for the Ardas. It remembers the dead. It asks for strength. And then it ends the way every Ardas has ended for a very long time: with two words about rising. Today: how the panth remembers.
screen: `EARLY JUNE, EARLY NOVEMBER.` → `SLOW KIRTAN, PHOTOGRAPHS.` → `EVERYONE STANDS.`

segments.voice: The panth, the Sikh community, remembers 1984 with practices it already had. Each June, Sikhs gather at the Akal Takht and in gurdwaras around the world to mark what many call Ghallughara Divas, the day of the massacre. Each November, there are gatherings for the families of those killed, with names read and stories told. At the center of both are two old practices. Kirtan: singing the Guru's hymns, so grief is held inside the Guru's words rather than left alone. And the Ardas. You know its shape now. Long before 1984, the Ardas already remembered Sikhs who suffered terribly and did not give up their faith: the ones who were tortured, broken, cut apart, and still kept their Sikhi. In it, the community's grief always has a place. You met chardi kala on the day about starting again. Here is the whole closing line, in Punjabi, the same every time: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Roughly: through Nanak, through the Name, may our spirits rise; by your will, may everyone be well. Notice what that ending does, on the day of remembering a massacre. It doesn't end on anger. It ends on chardi kala, rising spirits, and on sarbat da bhala, the good of all. All. Not just us. That is the panth's answer. It doesn't mean forgetting, or pretending justice was done. It means grief and hope standing in the same room, hands joined. This week, we went slowly: the crisis, June, the library, November, the long wait. It ends here, with rising spirits.
screen: `JUNE AND NOVEMBER GATHERINGS.` · `KIRTAN HOLDS THE GRIEF.` · `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THE MARTYRS.` · `IT ENDS: RISING SPIRITS, GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `RISING SPIRITS, EVEN HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end with the Ardas's last line. Settle, and let the whole week come to mind, gently. The pilgrims. The library. The names. The widows who waited. Breathe with them for a while. Then, if you'd like, say the line quietly, the way Sikhs end every Ardas: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. If you'd rather not say it, just hold its meaning: rising spirits, and good for everyone. Then rest. The bell holds the time.

Kirtan. Singing the Guru's hymns, so grief is held inside the Guru's words — part of how the panth remembers, with Ardas and gatherings each June and November, ending in chardi kala and the good of all.
Your line: rising spirits, even here. Today, after something heavy, do one small thing that lifts: a walk, a song, a kind word to someone. Day three hundred twelve.

313.title: Leaving Punjab
313.hook: from the late 1800s Sikhs went as soldiers, police and workers to Malaya, Hong Kong and East Africa
313.howItsDone: Wherever Sikhs settle, they install the Guru Granth Sahib in a room or building and gather for kirtan and langar; many of the oldest gurdwaras abroad began this way in Asia and East Africa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan: Ardas, and your line, rising spirits, even here. That closed our hardest week. Today we step outside Punjab, and follow Sikhs out into the wide world. Day three hundred thirteen.

Old photographs of Hong Kong, from about a hundred years ago, show tall policemen in turbans directing traffic. In Singapore and Malaya, the same: Sikh police and watchmen. In Kenya and Uganda, Punjabi workers laid the railway line through the bush toward Lake Victoria. How did a farming people from one corner of India end up across Asia and Africa? And when they got there, far from any gurdwara, what did they bring with them? Today: leaving Punjab.
screen: `TURBANED POLICE IN HONG KONG.` → `A RAILWAY THROUGH EAST AFRICA.` → `WHAT DID THEY CARRY?`

segments.voice: After the British took Punjab in 1849, they began recruiting Sikhs into their army in great numbers. Sikhs served across the empire. And the empire needed more than soldiers. It needed police for its port cities, guards for its banks and docks, and workers for its railways. So from the late 1800s, young Punjabi men, many of them Sikh, went out: as police to Hong Kong and Shanghai, as police and watchmen to Singapore and the Malay states, and as builders and craftsmen to East Africa, where tens of thousands of workers from India laid the Uganda Railway. Most went to earn and send money home. Many meant to return. Some did. Others stayed, married, and built lives. The Punjabi word for this is pardes, a foreign land, and pardesi, one who is far from home. There are Punjabi folk songs full of longing for the pardesi who went away. Now the line: carrying the guru abroad. Wherever a few Sikhs gathered, they did something simple. They set aside a room, installed the Guru Granth Sahib with respect, and began to sing. A corner of a police barracks, a rented room, later a proper building. That is all a gurdwara needs: the Guru, and a sangat. So some of the earliest gurdwaras abroad rose in these places, around the start of the twentieth century. The Sikhs who left Punjab did not leave the Guru behind. They took the Guru with them, carried with respect, and made a new home wherever the Guru rested.
screen: `RECRUITED ACROSS THE EMPIRE.` · `POLICE, WATCHMEN, RAILWAY BUILDERS.` · `PARDES: A FOREIGN LAND.` · `A ROOM, THE GURU, A SANGAT.` · then, large: `CARRYING THE GURU ABROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of someone who moved for work. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who left home to earn a living: a parent, a grandparent, a colleague, the person who cleans your office, the one who delivers your food. Picture where they came from, the place they miss, the people they send money to. Then ask what they might have carried with them, something you can't see. A faith, a song, a way of cooking. Hold them warmly. The bell holds the time.
Leaving Punjab. From the late 1800s, Sikhs went out as soldiers, police and workers to Malaya, Hong Kong and East Africa, and took the Guru with them.
Your line: carrying the guru abroad. Today, ask someone who moved far from home what they brought with them that they still keep. Day three hundred thirteen.

314.title: Sawmills of British Columbia
314.hook: in the early 1900s Sikh men worked sawmills and railways on Canada's west coast
314.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, honest work, as one of the three pillars of Sikh life; in Canada, the early mill workers' gurdwaras in Vancouver and Abbotsford are remembered as the community's beginnings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaving Punjab: police in Hong Kong, railway builders in East Africa, and your line, carrying the guru abroad. Today some of those men keep going east, across the Pacific, into the forests of Canada. Day three hundred fourteen.

Wet cedar, wood smoke, the scream of the blade: a sawmill in the rain. It's about 1906, on the coast of British Columbia. On the mill floor, among the other workers, are men in turbans, a long way from the wheat fields of Punjab. Some had heard about Canada in Hong Kong, where the ships for Vancouver set out. The pay was good, the work was hard, and the forests seemed endless. Today: the sawmills of British Columbia.
screen: `WET CEDAR AND WOOD SMOKE.` → `TURBANS ON THE MILL FLOOR.` → `ABOUT 1906.`

segments.voice: In the first years of the 1900s, a few thousand men from Punjab, nearly all of them Sikh, arrived on Canada's west coast. They worked in sawmills and logging camps, cleared land and laid track for the railways. It was heavy, dangerous work, often for lower pay than other workers got. And they met hostility. Many white residents wanted Asian immigrants kept out. In 1907, British Columbia took away the vote from people of South Asian origin. From 1908, Canada used a rule that immigrants had to arrive by a continuous journey from their home country, a rule that was almost impossible to meet from India. Immigration nearly stopped. The men who were already there held on. They lived together to save money, sent pay home, and did what Sikhs do: they built gurdwaras. In Vancouver in 1908, the Khalsa Diwan Society opened one of the first gurdwaras in North America. In 1911, Sikhs in Abbotsford, nearby, built a gurdwara with lumber from the mills and their own hands, and it still stands today, the oldest surviving gurdwara in North America. A Sikh mill owner later even founded a whole mill town on Vancouver Island and named it Paldi, after his village in Punjab. Behind all of it is an old Sikh value you already know: kirat karni, earning an honest living by your own work. Guru Nanak farmed. These men milled lumber. Honest work, far away, done with the Guru close by.
screen: `A FEW THOUSAND MEN FROM PUNJAB.` · `HOSTILITY, AND A CLOSED DOOR.` · `GURDWARAS BUILT FROM MILL LUMBER.` · `KIRAT KARNI: HONEST WORK.` · then, large: `HONEST WORK, FAR AWAY.`

If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If not, just send them a silent thank you. The bell holds the time.
Kirat. Honest labor — in the early 1900s, Sikh men did it in the mills and railways of Canada's west coast, and built gurdwaras from the lumber.
Your line: honest work, far away. Today, say a real thank you to one worker you usually pass without a word. Day three hundred fourteen.

315.title: Stockton, 1912
315.hook: Sikh farmworkers open the first gurdwara in the United States in California
315.carry: a door in a new land
315.howItsDone: Gurdwaras across the United States welcome visitors to kirtan and langar; the Stockton gurdwara, the oldest in the country, still serves a sangat today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirat: gurdwaras built from mill lumber, and your line, honest work, far away. Today we go south, down the coast, to the farms of California. Day three hundred fifteen.

California's Central Valley, about 1910. Flat fields to the horizon, heat shimmering off the dirt. Men from Punjab, many of them Sikh, have come down from Canada and across from Asia to work the farms: picking fruit, clearing land, laying irrigation ditches. It's familiar work. Punjab means five rivers, and these are farmers who know water and soil. But on a Sunday, there's nowhere to go. The nearest gurdwara is far up the coast in Vancouver, days away by train. So a few of them decide to make one. Today: Stockton.

segments.voice: In 1912, Sikh farmworkers formed the Pacific Coast Khalsa Diwan Society and opened a gurdwara in Stockton, a farm town in the Central Valley. It was the first gurdwara in the United States. It began modestly, and years later a new building went up beside the first. For decades it was the only one in the country, the place Sikhs traveled to from all over the West for gurpurabs, weddings and news from home. Think about the word gurdwara. Gur, the Guru. Dwara, a door. The Guru's door. And that's exactly what Stockton was: a door in a new land. Through it, lonely men found a sangat, a hot meal at langar, a bed for the night. Through it, too, came politics. Some Sikhs and other Indians in California were campaigning for India's freedom from British rule, and Stockton's gurdwara became a meeting place for them. Life outside the door was hard. Laws kept most Indian women from coming, and restricted who the men could marry and whether they could own land. In southern California, many Punjabi men married Mexican women, and their children grew up in families that mixed Punjabi and Spanish, gurdwara and church. Their children were sometimes called Mexican-Hindus, and some of them came to Stockton for the big gatherings. Looking back at this week: the library that was lost, November 1984, the long wait, how the panth remembers, leaving Punjab, the sawmills, and now Stockton. From loss, to a door opened in a new land.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a gurdwara near you. If you have your phone, look up the nearest gurdwara to where you are right now. Just find it on a map. Notice how far it is, and what street it's on. You don't have to go. Then put the phone down, settle, and breathe. Picture its door, open, with shoes lined up outside and someone serving tea inside. Think of the farmworkers in Stockton who made the first one. The bell holds the time.
Stockton. The California farm town where Sikh farmworkers opened the first gurdwara in the United States, in 1912.

Your line: a door in a new land. Today, when you walk through a door you take for granted, at home, at work or at a place you love, think of who first built it, and who it lets in. Day three hundred fifteen.
